paras: The attempted lynching of Monroe Wilkinson took place at Scottsville, Allen County, Kentucky, on the night of Sunday, September 23, 1888, when a party of about forty Black men twice tried to take Wilkinson from the town jail and hang him. Wilkinson, a Black man, was accused of shooting an elderly Black man in the back during a church service. The attackers were driven off, and the story ran nationally as a wire item about a murder in a church and a lynching threatened by Black residents.

According to a Louisville dispatch of September 25, Wilkinson, described as "a notorious negro," entered a colored church in Scottsville during a Saturday service, drew a revolver and broke up the congregation by threatening to shoot. An aged and "highly respected" colored man, whose name the papers gave as Berry Marion, Barry Merriman or Berry Manion, led him out of the church and remonstrated with him. As the old man turned away, Wilkinson was said to have shot him in the back, killing him instantly. The Weekly Courier-Journal, in its Kentucky news column, called Wilkinson "a drunken negro" and placed the killing at a colored Sunday-school meeting.

Wilkinson fled, but a posse of white and colored men pursued and captured him. The Black residents wanted to lynch him on the spot, but a white man took him up behind him on his horse and carried him to the jail at Scottsville; the Courier-Journal identified the rescuer as a lawyer.

On Sunday night a party of about forty Black men made two attempts to take Wilkinson from the jail and hang him, and both times they were driven off. The reports do not say who defended the jail. The would-be lynchers were said to have sworn that they would return with reinforcements and lynch him "at any cost," and the dispatch closed by noting that "much excitement" prevailed in the town.
A Wheeling digest of the wire reported that Wilkinson was still in jail. No report of a further attack, an inquest into the church killing, an indictment or a trial appears in the coverage.

The episode reached readers almost entirely through the Louisville wire of September 25, printed the same day in the Washington Evening Star, the Alexandria Gazette and the San Antonio Daily Light and the next day in papers in Indianapolis, New York, Memphis and Wheeling. Some editors headlined the killing, as in "Negro Commits Murder in a Church" and "An Unprovoked Murder," while others headlined the threat, as in the Indianapolis Journal's "Lynching Threatened" and the Evening Star's "Trying to Lynch a Murderer," subheaded "A Mob Thirsting for the Blood of the Slayer of an Aged Negro." The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer ran it as "At Any Cost. Negroes Swear They Will Lynch a Black Desperado."

Several copies, including the Alexandria Gazette and the New York Sun, stopped at Wilkinson's arrival at the jail and omitted the attacks on it. Weekly digests compressed the story into a sentence or two, and the Westminster Democratic Advocate reported "three unsuccessful efforts" rather than two. None of the papers commented on the attempt, and all treated Wilkinson's guilt as settled, calling him "the murderer" or "the rascal."

Most copies of the wire placed the shooting on Saturday, but the Memphis Appeal said "last Sunday," and the Courier-Journal's mention of a Sunday-school meeting also points to a Sunday. The full wire text, which gives two attempts on the jail, is closer to the original report than the later weekly item that gives three.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Monroe Wilkinson
bases: A party of about forty Black men twice tried to take the accused murderer Monroe Wilkinson from the Scottsville jail to hang him and were driven off, an attempted lynching [A1][A4].

A group of about forty acting on the accusation of murder tried without lawful authority to take Wilkinson from jail and hang him, but they were driven off and no report says he was killed [A1][A4][A7]; this was an attempted lynching.

The Louisville wire [A1][A4] and a separately worded Kentucky item in the Weekly Courier-Journal [A10] agree that Wilkinson shot an old Black man at a church gathering and that Black residents wanted to hang him; the two jail attempts appear only in the wire and papers condensing it [A1][A4][A7][A9].

accounts.label: Louisville wire
accounts.gist: Wilkinson broke up a church service with a revolver and shot the old man who led him out; a mixed posse captured him, a white man carried him to jail, and about forty Black men twice tried to take him out and hang him Sunday night but were driven off.

accounts.label: Kentucky items column
accounts.gist: A 'drunken negro' killed an old man at a colored Sunday-school meeting; the Black residents would have hanged him had a lawyer not taken him to jail on his horse.

framing.detail: Papers ran the Louisville wire under headlines stressing the murder ('Negro Commits Murder in a Church', 'An Unprovoked Murder', 'A Desperado in a Church') or the lynching threat ('Lynching Threatened', 'Trying to Lynch a Murderer').

The Wheeling Daily Intelligencer's 'At Any Cost. Negroes Swear They Will Lynch a Black Desperado' and the Evening Star's 'A Mob Thirsting for the Blood' subhead foregrounded the would-be lynchers without condemning them.
The Weekly Courier-Journal called Wilkinson 'the rascal' and credited a lawyer with preventing the hanging.

conflicts.note: Variant spellings of one name across reprints of a single wire and one Kentucky item; no version is clearly better.
Most wire copies say Saturday; the Memphis Appeal's 'last Sunday' may be a copying variant.
The full wire text says two; 'three' appears only in a later weekly condensation.
